title: Adaptive Headroom Leasing and Tenant Staggering PRD
creator: Priya Raman
description: Problem: Dedicated tenants occasionally experience noisy bursts and hotspot patterns that cause latency spikes for neighbors or force aggressive preemption. Fixed reservation models either waste headroom or allow unfair burst capture. This PRD proposes an Adaptive Headroom Leasing mechanism combined with Tenant Staggering windows to allocate short-term, lease-based extra capacity to tenants while reducing contention and improving tail latency for the fleet.
goals: 1) Provide tenant-configurable short-term headroom leases (duration and max qps/token capacity) that can be automatically granted based on observed burst patterns and tenant entitlement. 2) Implement a staggered prewarm/lease schedule so simultaneous warmups for many tenants are avoided. 3) Integrate leasing with autoscaling and fallback so leased headroom is reclaimed gracefully on pressure. 4) Expose control plane UI and API for lease policies, visibility, and audit logs.
non_goals: 1) This is not a replacement for long-term reserved capacity contracts. 2) We will not implement a marketplace or monetary exchange for leasing in this phase. 3) We will not change model pinning or model variant fallback logic beyond respecting lease-aware routing.
requirements: Headroom lease object exposed in Console and API with parameters: lease_id, tenant_id, max_rps, max_tokens_per_minute, duration_secs, prewarm_flag, priority_tier
Server-side runtime support to accept & enforce active leases per tenant across routing layer and dedicated GPU pool schedulers
Staggering algorithm to compute prewarm windows per tenant to avoid correlated warmups in the same zone/cluster
Lease allocator service with controls: reactive (on burst trigger), scheduled (time-based), and manual grant via Console or API
Telemetry: per-lease metrics (granted_bytes, used_bytes, peak_latency_during_lease, eviction_count) and audit logs for grant/revoke actions
Failover behavior: automatic revocation or reduction of lease if GPU pressure crosses defined thresholds; transparent fallback to reserved baseline or shared pool
Rollout controls: feature flag gating per org and per-zone with percentage-based canary
Acceptance tests and load tests demonstrating tail-latency improvement and reduced cross-tenant impact
RBAC: only admins and billing or support roles can manually grant permanent leases
Quota impact: leases must respect customer entitlement and billing metrics must track leased usage separately
acceptance_criteria: API: Create/Update/Delete lease endpoints respond with correct validation and persist lease metadata
Console: Lease UI present in Dedicated > Capacity page with create/modify workflows and audit trail
Runtime: During a synthetic burst test, granting a lease to tenant A increases A's throughput in line with lease limits without causing >10% increase in p95 latency for co-located tenants
Staggering: When 100 tenants request prewarm within the same minute, the staggering algorithm schedules warmups across windows such that simultaneous prewarm concurrency <= 10% of pool size
Reclamation: Under sustained GPU pressure (>90% utilization for 30s), active leases are revoked or throttled and requests route to fallback within 10s
Telemetry: Lease metrics are emitted to telemetry pipeline and visible in Console within 2 minutes of lease activity
Security: Lease create/modify/delete actions are logged and require appropriate RBAC checks; security review sign-off obtained
E2E tests: Automated integration tests exercising grant, use, revoke, and fallback succeed in CI for dedicated clusters
success_metrics: Reduce cross-tenant p95 latency incidents attributable to correlated warmups by 60% in first 90 days
Decrease cold-start token overhead per burst by 30% for tenants using prewarm leases
Less than 1% of lease grants resulting in emergency revocation in steady state
Telemetry coverage: 100% of lease events have corresponding audit records and metrics
rollout_plan: Phase 1: Implement API, lease allocator prototype, and runtime stubs behind feature flag in canary cluster (4 weeks). Phase 2: Console + telemetry + RBAC + controlled alpha with 5 pilot customers (6 weeks). Phase 3: Autoscale integration, eviction tuning, and wider beta for internal Dedicated tenants (4 weeks). Phase 4: General availability with documentation and runbook (2 weeks). Each phase gated by SLO and safety tests.

open_questions: Should leases be charged differently than reserved or pay-as-you-go usage in billing model?
What is the max allowed lease duration before it must be converted to a reservation?
Do we allow a tenant to hold multiple overlapping leases? If yes, how are priorities merged?
How to surface denied lease requests to tenants and provide remediation suggestions?
Do we expose an SLA for leases or mark them explicitly as best-effort?
engineering_notes: Allocator is a best-effort controller that coordinates with the routing layer and node schedulers. Implementation will prefer token-bucket enforcement at the edge and soft admission control in the scheduler. Prewarm staging should avoid aggressive KV cache rewrites; prefer graceful warming using small ramp-up RTs. Autoscale integration must provide a fast revoke API and a status endpoint for lease health.
qa_plan: Unit tests for API validation, integration tests for allocator <-> runtime, chaos tests that simulate noisy neighbor bursts and forced revocation, performance tests to verify no more than 10% p95 increase for co-tenants under lease activity, nightly e2e run in staging cluster with synthetic tenants.
monitoring_alerts: Alert if >5% of active leases revoked in 5m window
Alert if prewarm concurrency exceeds safe window threshold for a pool
Alert if per-tenant latency deviates >20% after lease grant
notes: This mechanism complements existing reserved capacity and soft-eviction policies. The product decision favors protecting fleet tail latency while giving tenants predictable short-term capacity for bursty workloads. Security review must evaluate audit trail completeness and abuse vectors (e.g., denial by over-requesting prewarms).
